facts.statement: The study followed 1,370 community-dwelling people who were at least 65 years old for a period of four years.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Researchers measured the amount of the protein Tsukushi in the blood of participants at the start of the study.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: People who had lower amounts of Tsukushi in their blood at the beginning were more likely to develop sarcopenia later on.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The link between low Tsukushi levels and the risk of sarcopenia was stronger for women than for men.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Using Tsukushi levels by itself helped predict future muscle loss with moderate accuracy, but adding other clinical factors improved the prediction score.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Before this study, there was no prior forward-looking clinical proof that blood levels of Tsukushi connect to the development of sarcopenia.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The researchers used specific statistical tools to check if the relationship between protein levels and risk followed a straight line or a curve, and to test how well the protein could predict future outcomes.
facts.subject: humans
